title: ayam atma brahma — a week each
hook: three sounds, one silence, and two schools that hear it differently
carry: ayam atma brahma — a week each
tomorrow: why does an Upanishad stop to talk about honey?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ayam atma brahma came through the back door: neti neti, not this, not this. Today the Mandukya gives the same self a sound, and then takes the sound away.

A phone call ends, and for a second after the voice stops, the room sounds louder than before. Say Om slowly and the same thing happens: ah, then oo, then the hum of mmm against closed lips. Three sounds. Then it stops, and there's a beat of nothing. The Mandukya Upanishad says that beat is the fourth part, the heart of the whole teaching. Two great schools of Vedanta agree on that much. They don't agree on what lives in the silence.
screen: `A ROOM LOUDER AFTER THE CALL.` → `AH, OO, MMM, THEN NOTHING.` → `TWO SCHOOLS, ONE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the text. The Mandukya lays this self over Om. A is waking, the self that deals with the world outside. U is dreaming, at home in an inner world. M is deep sleep, where everything gathers into one. And the fourth has no sound part at all. It is peaceful, kind, not two. That, the text says, is the self. Now the two readings, each in its own voice. Advaita teachers read the Mandukya through verses tradition credits to Gaudapada, and through Shankara. For them, the fourth is the one self that was there all along. Waking, dream and sleep pass across it like weather across the sky, and not two means just that: there is no second thing. Madhva's school reads the same Upanishad and hears the Lord in it. The quarters, it says, name forms of Vishnu, who is present in waking, dream and sleep and stands beyond them all. The self who knows him is real, depends on him, and never becomes him. Both schools take the Mandukya as scripture. Both chant the same Om. One hears the silence as the self with nothing beside it; the other hears a presence holding everything that is.
screen: `A, U, M: WAKING, DREAM, SLEEP.` · `THE FOURTH: PEACEFUL, NOT TWO.` · `ADVAITA: ONE SELF, NO SECOND.` · `MADHVA: THE LORD, BEYOND ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: If you're somewhere you can, say Om once, slowly, out loud: ah, oo, mmm. Then stay in the silence after it for a few breaths before the next one. Keep going at your own pace, listening as closely to the quiet as to the sound.
Ayam atma brahma, through the Mandukya: Om's three sounds as waking, dream and sleep, and a fourth that makes no sound, peaceful, kind, not two.
Something to keep: ayam atma brahma — a week each, three sounds and a silence two schools listen to. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Om is chanted at the start and end of prayers and study; students of the Mandukya chant it slowly and rest in the silence after it, and teachers of different Vedanta schools explain that silence in their own ways.

original.note: Sanskrit: the sacred syllable, which the Mandukya hears as A, U, M and a silence.

trapdoor: what you thought: Om is one long sound.
what it means: three sounds for waking, dream and sleep, and a soundless fourth called the self.
what a scholar hears: Mandukya 8–12; Advaita reads it with the verses ascribed to Gaudapada and with Shankara, while Madhva reads the quarters as forms of Vishnu.

chat.meaning: Advaita reads the silent fourth as the one self, not two; Madhva's school reads the quarters as forms of the Lord. Both take the Mandukya as scripture.

Mandukya.meaning: a short Upanishad that lays the self over the sound Om

Gaudapada.meaning: a teacher tradition credits with verses on the Mandukya

Madhva.meaning: founder of a Vedanta school that keeps God and self distinct

Vishnu.meaning: the god Madhva's school worships as the Lord

sources.ref: Mandukya Upanishad 1–2 (Om is all this; this self is Brahman; the self has four quarters)
Mandukya Upanishad 7–12 (the fourth: peaceful, kind, not two; A, U and M as waking, dream and deep sleep; the fourth without a sound part)
Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya and Shankara's commentary (Advaita reading, summarized); Madhva's commentary on the Mandukya (the quarters as forms of Vishnu, summarized)
